notes.decision: The numeral 15 marks the start of Chapter 15. Lines 22-25 constitute the chapter heading apparatus (number + title) before the narrative incipit at line 26.
The recurring Kephalaia opening formula 'Once again, as the Illuminator was sitting...' Editor's restoration confirmed by countless parallel chapter incipits. ⲍⲙⲉⲥⲧ is qualitative of ϩⲙⲟⲟⲥ 'sit.'

'Two substances' — the foundational Manichaean dualistic teaching. ⲥⲛ̄ⲧⲉ is the feminine numeral 'two,' agreeing with feminine ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲁ. The disciples respond after the Illuminator's discourse on the two substances.

'Death has risen to plant himself / stand firm.' ⲧⲱⲛⲉ = 'rise up'; ⲧⲱⲕ ⲁⲣⲉⲧ⸗ idiom = 'stand fast, plant oneself.' This is the disciples' question/observation that prompts the Illuminator's teaching in this chapter.

Translated as 'kind' throughout. The word functions enumeratively in this kephalaion: 'first kind' (l.3), 'fourth kind' (l.14), 'twelve kinds' (l.31-32, in chapter heading). Likely Lycopolitan reflex of ⲧⲱϣ/ⲧⲱⲉ ('division, tribe, district, category') with regular ⲱ→ⲁ vowel shift. Could alternatively be 'category, type, division.' The chapter heading 'mystery of the twelve kinds that came to be in the darkness' (l.31-32) confirms this is a cosmological enumeration term — possibly the Manichaean equivalent of γένη ('kinds, races') of darkness.

notes.coptic_form: ⲧϯⲉ ⲛⲧⲁⲓ̈ⲉ ⲍⲁⲩⲧ ⲙⲛ̄ ⲧϯⲉ ⲛⲛⲉⲥⲍⲁⲙⲉ
notes.decision: Translated as 'the portion of the male kinds with the portion of the female ones.' The word ⲧϯⲉ is uncertain: it could be (1) ϯⲡⲉ 'kind, taste, manner' (already in vocabulary), giving 'the kind/type of the male kinds'; (2) Lyc form for 'half/portion' (cf. ⲡⲁϣⲉ); or (3) ϯⲟⲩ 'five' (but spelling differs from ⲡϯⲟⲩ used elsewhere on this page). 'Portion' fits the cosmological context of male/female cosmic divisions within each kind.

Translated as 'trees' — interpreted as Lycopolitan reflex of ϣⲏⲛ ('tree') in collective/plural reading, agreeing with the plural relative ⲛⲉⲧⲁⲩⲃⲉⲃⲉ ('those that gushed forth'). May be the surviving fragment of a longer compound ⲛⲱⲏϣⲛ whose first part fell in the lacuna at end of line 6. Standard schema (five trees of death = five worlds) supports the plural reading.

Parsed across the line break as a verbal continuation: ⲁ-(ϥ)-ⲥⲁⲣϩ 'and (it/he) spread forth' or similar perfect form of ⲥⲱⲣ 'spread, scatter,' with subject = ⲡⲙⲟⲩ ('death') from the relative clause, or possibly the five creatures. The same verb ⲁⲥⲥⲁⲣⲥ̄ ('she spread forth') appears in line 17 with Matter as subject. The ⲁϩ-/ⲁ(ⲥ)- alternation may reflect Lycopolitan orthography or a third masculine reference back to death.

Translated 'they fixed him for ever.' The verb ⲧⲁⲭⲁϩ = ⲧⲁⲭⲟ + ϥ (Greek-derived τάσσω 'appoint, fix, ordain'); ϣⲁⲁⲛⲏⲍⲉ = ϣⲁ ⲉⲛⲉϩ 'forever, for ever and ever.' In the context of the cosmic capture of dark powers, this likely refers to the eternal binding/sealing of either the dark figure or some captive light-element.

Translated 'giving glory' — analyzed as ϯ + ⲉⲁⲩ ('give glory, glorify'). The construction with ⲉⲙⲛ̄ ('there was no...') likely means 'while there was no [one] giving glory' — a primordial state before glorification existed.

Translated 'Therefore in the manner of the land of darkness — namely.' ⲭⲉ here introduces the explicative content — the spirit and (...) of the dark land. The construction frames lines 24-26 as an exegetical reading of the cosmological structure just enumerated.

Translated 'Some' as indefinite plural subject of ⲥⲉⲧⲏⲕ (3pl). Lycopolitan ⲟⲩⲉ functions like ⲟⲩⲟⲛ 'some, certain ones' before a 3pl verb. The opponents are unspecified persecutors — the parallel structure of the page (Second Living Man : Apostle :: First Man : cosmogonic First Man) makes them rival groups within or against the Church.

'The Second Living Man' — apostolic figure (probably Mani or his apostolic predecessor), parallel to the cosmogonic First Man (ⲡϣⲁⲣⲡ ⲛ̄ⲣⲱⲙⲉ) of line 4. The typological structure: just as the First Man humbled the Darkness in primordial cosmogony, the Second (apostolic) Man is persecuted in the Church.
Read as Lyc ϯⲃⲓⲟ 'humbled, abased.' Causative-perfective: 'the First Man humbled the Darkness' — the cosmogonic victory expressed as humiliation/abasement of the dark powers.
